item.title: Scientists engineer bacteria to produce molecules using light
item.description:
Researchers at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign have engineered bacteria that can manufacture novel molecules when activated by light, marking what scientists describe as the first integration of light-driven enzymatic reactions into cellular metabolism. The proof-of-concept study, published this week in Nature Catalysis, could expand the range of compounds that can be sustainably produced through biomanufacturing.

The technology works by equipping Escherichia coli bacteria with artificial photoenzymes—light-activated catalysts capable of performing chemical reactions that natural enzymes cannot achieve. When illuminated, these engineered bacteria can convert glucose into higher-value chemical products without requiring costly external materials.

item.title: Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS nears Jupiter flyby after archival data reveals early presence
item.description:
Scientists have confirmed that the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS was captured in space-based observations nearly two months before its official discovery on July 1, 2025, underscoring questions about how automated detection systems process vast astronomical datasets. The revelation comes as the interstellar visitor approaches a close pass with Jupiter in mid-March that researchers say could expose new secrets about its composition and structure.

According to newly confirmed analyses, 3I/ATLAS appeared in data collected by NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) between May 7 and June 2, 2025—55 days before the ATLAS telescope in Chile flagged the object as a potential interstellar visitor. The comet remained effectively invisible in those earlier recordings until scientists revisited the data with updated parameters and image-stacking techniques, coadding more than 9,000 individual frames to reconstruct a faint but consistent signal matching the object's trajectory.

item.title: Particle accelerator decodes lost ancient Greek star catalog
item.description:
Powerful X-rays from a particle accelerator have illuminated fragments of one of history's most important astronomical documents—the lost star catalog of the ancient Greek astronomer Hipparchus—after lying hidden beneath medieval religious texts for more than a millennium.

Researchers working at SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory in Menlo Park, California, this month successfully decoded erased ancient Greek text from a manuscript known as the Codex Climaci Rescriptus, including star coordinates that date back more than 2,000 years.

item.title: Japan, UK launch cyber partnership amid China tensions
item.description:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and British Prime Minister Keir Starmer agreed Saturday to deepen cooperation on cybersecurity, defense, and critical mineral supply chains during talks in Tokyo, as both nations seek to counter China's growing influence in the Indo-Pacific region.

The summit at the Prime Minister's Office concluded with the announcement of a new Japan-UK Strategic Cyber Partnership aimed at detecting, deterring, and defending against cyber threats from foreign adversaries. The two leaders also affirmed the urgent need for like-minded nations to strengthen supply chains for essential minerals, with China's recent export restrictions on rare earth elements adding urgency to the discussions.

item.title: Ukraine grid failure triggers Chornobyl power loss, blackouts
item.description:
Ukrainian nuclear power plants temporarily reduced their output Saturday morning after a technical malfunction triggered a cascading failure across the country's power grid, forcing Chornobyl to briefly lose all off-site power, the International Atomic Energy Agency reported.

The disruption, which also caused widespread blackouts in neighboring Moldova, struck at 10:42 a.m. local time when a 750-kilovolt line between western and central Ukraine and a 400-kilovolt line connecting Romania and Moldova simultaneously shut down, according to Ukrainian Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal. The failure activated automatic protection systems at substations and forced nuclear plant units to unload their power, leading to emergency outages across multiple regions including Kyiv and Kharkiv.

item.title: Waymo seeks $16B funding round at nearly $110B valuation
item.description:
Alphabet Inc.'s autonomous driving unit Waymo is aiming to raise about $16 billion in a financing round that would value the robotaxi company at nearly $110 billion, according to people familiar with the matter, as reported by Bloomberg News on Saturday.

The parent company would provide about $13 billion to the robotaxi firm, while the rest would come from new investors including Sequoia Capital, DST Global, and Dragoneer Investment Group, said the sources, who asked not to be identified because the discussions are private.

item.title: Hyundai CEO outlines $26B U.S. expansion amid tariff pressure
item.description:
José Muñoz, the first non-Korean leader of any major Korean conglomerate, is doubling down on America even as tariffs and shifting electric vehicle policies roil the auto industry.

In an interview with The Wall Street Journal released Friday, the Hyundai Motor president and CEO outlined his vision to localize production and deploy humanoid robots as the South Korean automaker navigates trade tensions with Washington.

"America is the most important market for Hyundai," Muñoz said, adding that the company wants "at least 80% of what we sell in the US" to be produced domestically. "This is the best recipe to be successful and to not be dependent on policies."

item.title: Danish veterans march on US embassy over Trump NATO remarks
item.description:
Veterans and officials throughout the NATO alliance have reacted with fury to President Donald Trump's claim that allied forces "stayed a little back, a little off the front lines" during the Afghanistan War, with Danish veterans organizing a protest march on the US embassy in Copenhagen on Saturday.

Trump sparked the controversy during a January 22 interview with Fox News in Davos, Switzerland, questioning NATO's reliability and asserting that the United States had "never needed" its allies. "We have never really asked anything of them," Trump said. "They'll say they sent some troops to Afghanistan or this or that. And they did — they stayed a little back, a little off the front lines."

The remarks drew immediate backlash given that 457 British, 158 Canadian, and 44 Danish service members were killed during the two-decade Afghanistan conflict — after NATO invoked Article 5, its mutual defense clause, for the first and only time following the September 11 attacks.

item.title: NASA begins Artemis 2 countdown after cold weather delay
item.description:
A rare arctic outbreak sweeping through Florida has forced NASA to postpone the first crewed lunar mission in more than half a century, tightening an already narrow launch window for the Artemis II mission.

NASA announced Friday that the first possible launch date for Artemis II is now no earlier than February 8, two days later than originally planned, after sub-freezing temperatures at Kennedy Space Center made a critical fueling test impossible to conduct this weekend. The agency had intended to perform the "wet dress rehearsal" of its 322-foot Space Launch System rocket on Saturday but canceled the operation late Thursday.

item.title: Trump says India will buy Venezuelan oil instead of Iran
item.description:
President Donald Trump announced Saturday that India will purchase oil from Venezuela rather than Iran, marking the latest development in Washington's broader effort to reshape global energy flows and reduce India's reliance on Russian crude.

"We've already established that agreement, the idea of the agreement," Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One while traveling from Washington, D.C., to Florida, according to Reuters. The president also said China is invited to negotiate a deal with the U.S. to purchase Venezuelan oil.

item.title: Slovakia's security adviser resigns over Epstein file links
item.description:
Slovakia's national security adviser Miroslav Lajčák resigned Saturday after newly released U.S. Justice Department files revealed his past communications with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, making him one of the first high-profile casualties of the massive document dump.

Prime Minister Robert Fico accepted Lajčák's resignation via a video statement on Facebook, describing the former diplomat as "an excellent diplomat" while defending him against media coverage he called exaggerated. Lajčák, who previously served as Slovakia's foreign minister and held a yearlong term as president of the United Nations General Assembly, said he stepped down to prevent political strain on the government rather than because of any criminal or unethical conduct.

item.title: Gaza's Rafah crossing begins trial operations after 2-year closure
item.description:
The Rafah border crossing between Gaza and Egypt began trial operations on Sunday, February 1, marking the first time the vital passageway has opened for pedestrian movement since Israeli forces captured the area in May 2024. The partial reopening completes a key component of the first phase of the US-brokered ceasefire agreement.

Under the arrangement, Israel will permit up to 150 Palestinians to leave Gaza daily, while only 50 will be allowed to enter, according to Israeli security officials. Full operations are expected to begin Monday following initial testing of security screening systems.

item.title: Trump says Iran 'seriously' negotiating as US naval buildup continues
item.description:
President Donald Trump announced Saturday that Iran is "seriously" engaged in negotiations with the United States, even as Washington maintains a naval armada off Iranian shores and both sides keep the specter of military conflict alive.

"They are talking to us, and we'll see if we can do something. Otherwise, we'll see what happens. We have a big fleet heading out there," Trump told Fox News on January 31. Speaking later to reporters aboard Air Force One, he added: "They are negotiating".

item.title: Musk says China's power output will triple US within a year
item.description:
Elon Musk sounded the alarm on China's energy dominance late last week, predicting that the country's electricity generation will soon exceed that of the United States by a factor of three, driven by a rapid expansion in solar power.

"China electricity generation is still growing super fast, with solar being the largest incremental contributor, and will exceed America by a factor of 3X either this year or next," Musk wrote on X on January 31. The Tesla and SpaceX CEO was responding to a report highlighting that China accounted for 33.2 percent of global electricity generation in 2025—more than double the US share of roughly 14.2 percent.

item.title: Pentagon delays Iran strikes to bolster Mideast air defenses
item.description:
The Pentagon is holding off on potential military action against Iran while it deploys additional air defense systems across the Middle East, U.S. officials told The Wall Street Journal on Sunday, as Washington prepares for the possibility of a broader conflict with Tehran.

While President Donald Trump's promised "armada," spearheaded by the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group, has arrived in the Arabian Sea, officials say a comprehensive offensive would require robust defensive coverage to protect American forces, Israel, and Arab allies from Iranian retaliation.

item.title: Zelenskyy confirms Ukraine-Russia talks for Feb. 4-5 in Abu Dhabi
item.description:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on Sunday that a new round of U.S.-brokered trilateral peace talks between Ukraine and Russia will take place in Abu Dhabi on February 4-5, with Kyiv ready for a "substantive discussion" on ending the nearly four-year war.

"Our negotiating team has just delivered a report. The dates for the next trilateral meetings have been set – February 4 and 5 in Abu Dhabi," Zelenskyy wrote on X. "Ukraine is ready for a substantive discussion, and we are interested in ensuring that the outcome brings us closer to a real and dignified end to the war."

item.title: Top US, Israeli generals meet at Pentagon amid Iran tensions
item.description: The top military commanders of the United States and Israel held closed-door talks at the Pentagon on Friday amid escalating tensions with Iran, according to two US officials who spoke to Reuters on the condition of anonymity. The previously unreported meeting between US General Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, and Israeli Defense Forces Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir comes as both nations coordinate potential military planning while President Donald Trump weighs strikes against the Islamic Republic.

item.title: Iran's Khamenei warns US attack would trigger regional war
item.description:
Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei issued his most direct warning to the United States on Sunday, declaring that any American military strike would escalate into a broader conflict engulfing the Middle East.

"The Americans should know that if they start a war, this time it will be a regional war," Khamenei said, according to Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency. The 86-year-old leader addressed a gathering in Tehran ahead of the anniversary of the 1979 Islamic Revolution, dismissing US military deployments as familiar posturing that would not intimidate Iranians.

item.title: Israel reopens Rafah crossing as Gaza ceasefire enters new phase
item.description: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's decision to join U.S. President Donald Trump's newly established Board of Peace continues to generate debate among international observers, as the initiative advances into its second phase of managing post-war Gaza while Netanyahu remains subject to an International Criminal Court arrest warrant.

item.title: Iran's top diplomat says nuclear deal achievable amid US standoff
item.description:
Iran's top diplomat expressed confidence Sunday that a nuclear deal with the United States remains achievable even as both nations inch toward potential military confrontation, highlighting a volatile standoff defined by simultaneous diplomacy and displays of force.

In an interview with CNN, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he believes Tehran can reach an agreement with Washington on its nuclear program—but only if trust can be rebuilt. "Unfortunately, we have lost our trust in the US as a negotiating partner," Araghchi told the network, while noting that "fruitful" mediation by regional partners is helping advance discussions.

His remarks came the same day Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei issued his sharpest warning yet to Washington, declaring that any American military strike would ignite "a regional war" across the Middle East.
